title: Unveiling the Power of the Exchange | Sicilian Defense  | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: Instead of the accelerated setup Black answers with the small pawn to d6 — the classical Sicilian move order, a window into how a grandmaster handles the opening he knows best.
moves.teaches: d6 keeps every classical Sicilian structure open — Najdorf, Scheveningen, Dragon — deferring the choice.
moves.plans: Develop flexibly and pick the structure later.

moves.spoken: The bishop checks from b5 — the Moscow, or Canal, Variation. Rather than the open Sicilian, White pins toward the king and invites a block.
moves.teaches: The Moscow (Bb5+) sidesteps mainline Sicilian theory by trading or provoking a block on d7.
moves.plans: Choose the block that keeps winning chances.

moves.spoken: The knight to d7 is the ambitious block. The bishop to d7 leads to a lot of draws and the queen to d7 to dry positions; the knight strikes the balance — sharp, playing for a win, yet not objectively dubious. It is the choice of top players pressing with Black.
moves.teaches: When choosing how to meet a check, weigh solidity against winning chances — the knight block keeps the game alive.
moves.plans: Develop behind the knight and keep the position rich.

moves.spoken: White grabs queenside space with the pawn to a4, a recently fashionable try that clamps down on Black's ...b5 expansion before it can start.
moves.teaches: A rook-pawn thrust like a4 is prophylaxis — it stops the opponent's freeing break in advance.
moves.plans: Ignore it and develop; the break can wait.

moves.spoken: The pawn to e6 sets up a Scheveningen structure — the flexible small-centre Sicilian. Black actively welcomes White playing d4, which simply hands over the very structure Black is aiming for.
moves.teaches: The Scheveningen's small pawn centre (d6/e6) is flexible and hard to attack — invite d4 to reach it.
moves.plans: Complete development and meet d4 with the standard recapture.

moves.spoken: White obliges with the pawn to d4, and the position becomes exactly the Sicilian structure Black wanted — a familiar open-Sicilian Scheveningen with a slightly better-placed white bishop as the only difference.
moves.teaches: Transposing into a structure you know beats fighting an unfamiliar one, even at a small objective cost.
moves.plans: Recapture, castle, and play the standard plans.

moves.spoken: Castling completes development into a clean open-Sicilian Scheveningen. There is no rush for ...a6 — the b5-bishop is not a real nuisance, and the move is saved for the moment it truly counts, the threat stronger than the execution.
moves.teaches: Hold a useful move in reserve — an unforced ...a6 spends a tempo the position may need later.
moves.plans: Finish the setup, keep ...a6 for the right moment.

moves.spoken: The queen settles on c7 — the move that completes the standard Sicilian formation. Nothing deep, just good development: the queen is better placed here, eyeing the c-file and supporting the central and queenside breaks.
moves.teaches: Queen to c7 is the natural finishing touch of the Scheveningen — c-file pressure and break support.
moves.plans: Prepare the ...d5 or ...b5 break from a fully developed position.
